summary: This standards-track RFC describes how a JSON Web Token can declare that its presenter holds a particular proof-of-possession key, and how the recipient can confirm that cryptographically. This helps prevent a stolen token from being used by someone else.

eli5.summary: A ticket works only if you can also show the secret key that goes with it. That way, if someone steals the ticket, they still can't use it.

questions: what is the jwt cnf claim
what is proof of possession in jwt
what is a holder of key token
how do i bind a jwt to a key
subtitle: How a JSON Web Token can say "only the holder of this key may use me", and how a recipient checks it.

tldr.problem: A plain JWT works for whoever holds it, so a stolen token can be replayed by someone else. The recipient needs a way to know the presenter also holds a particular key.
tldr.mechanism: The issuer adds a "cnf" (confirmation) claim to the JWT. Its members identify the proof-of-possession key: as a public key ("jwk"), an encrypted symmetric key ("jwe"), a key ID ("kid") or a key set URL ("jku"). The presenter then proves it holds the key.
tldr.outcome: The RFC deliberately leaves the proof step (for example signing a nonce) to other protocols. It registers the "cnf" claim and a new IANA registry of confirmation methods.

today: RFC 7800 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2016. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Holder-of-Key Idea
sections.content:
RFC 7800 describes how a JSON Web Token (JWT, see RFC 7519) can declare that the presenter of the JWT possesses a particular proof-of-possession (PoP) key, and how the recipient can cryptographically confirm that. Proving possession of a key is also called being a holder-of-key.

The RFC defines three roles. The issuer creates the JWT and binds the PoP key to it. The presenter proves possession of a private key (asymmetric) or secret key (symmetric) to a recipient. The recipient receives the JWT with the PoP key information from the presenter.

The RFC defines how to communicate confirmation key information in JWTs. It does not define the protocol that exercises the key.
sections.eli5: Think of a concert ticket with a secret handshake written on it. The ticket alone is not enough: you also have to know the handshake. The person who made the ticket, the person holding it and the guard at the door each have a name here.

sections.title: Symmetric and Asymmetric Use Cases
sections.content:
The introduction walks through two cases. With a symmetric key, either the presenter or the issuer generates the key and privately sends it to the other. The issuer puts an encrypted copy of the key in the confirmation claim, encrypted with a key known only to the issuer and the recipient. The whole JWT is integrity protected by the issuer. The presenter then shows the JWT and demonstrates the key, for example in a challenge/response protocol. The RFC compares this to the use of Kerberos tickets.

With an asymmetric key, the presenter generates a public/private key pair and sends the public key to the issuer. The issuer puts the public key (or an identifier for it) in the confirmation claim and protects the JWT with a digital signature. The presenter then uses the private key, for example in a TLS exchange or by signing a nonce, and the recipient checks that against the public key from the claim.

The RFC notes that a more secure practice is to derive the symmetric keys actually used from exchanged secrets with a Key Derivation Function, instead of using the exchanged secrets directly.
sections.eli5: There are two kinds of secret. A shared secret is a password only two people know. A key pair has a public half anyone can see and a private half you keep hidden, and only the private half can do the trick.

sections.title: The cnf Confirmation Claim
sections.content:
By including a cnf (confirmation) claim, the issuer declares that the presenter possesses a particular key and that the recipient can confirm it. The value is a JSON object whose members identify the PoP key.

The presenter is normally the subject named by the sub claim. If there is no sub, the presenter is normally the issuer named by iss. At least one of sub and iss MUST be present. An application may instead identify the presenter with an explicit claim such as azp, and the means of identifying the presenter is ultimately application specific.

The cnf value MUST represent only a single PoP key, so at most one of jwk, jwe and jku may be present. Members the implementation does not understand MUST be ignored unless the application requires otherwise. The set of confirmation members a JWT must contain is context dependent and outside the scope of the RFC.
sections.eli5: The cnf claim is a note on the ticket that says which secret goes with it. Only one secret may be named, and if the guard cannot read part of the note, the guard skips it.

sections.title: Four Ways to Name the Key
sections.content:
Each way of identifying the key is a member of the cnf object.

  • jwk: a JSON Web Key holding the public key that matches the presenter's private key. It MUST contain the required members for its key type and MAY contain others such as kid. It may also hold a symmetric key, but only if the JWT is encrypted; otherwise the symmetric key MUST be encrypted as in jwe.
  • jwe: a symmetric key as a JWK, encrypted to a key known to the recipient using the JWE Compact Serialization. The UTF-8 encoding of the JWK is the JWE plaintext.
  • kid: a key ID, usable when the recipient can obtain the identified key from it. The content of the value is application specific; some applications may use a JWK Thumbprint.
  • jku: a URI pointing to a JWK Set that contains the key. If the set holds several keys, a matching kid MUST also be included.

For jku, the protocol used to fetch the resource MUST provide integrity protection. An HTTP GET for the JWK Set MUST use TLS, and the server identity MUST be validated.
sections.eli5: The note can hold the key itself, a locked box with the key inside, just a name tag for the key, or an address where the key can be looked up. You pick one of the four.

sections.title: What the RFC Leaves Out
sections.content:
Proof of possession is typically shown by having the presenter sign a value chosen by the recipient, often called a nonce or a challenge. The RFC intentionally does not describe how the nonce is sent, what it contains or how the signed nonce comes back, because different protocols do this differently.

For a symmetric key, another way to prove possession is to encrypt the key to the recipient, and how the recipient obtains its key is also protocol specific. The RFC points to the OAuth 2.0 PoP Security Architecture draft for examples.
sections.eli5: The RFC says what is written on the ticket, but not how the guard tests your secret handshake. Each place can invent its own test.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
All the security considerations of RFC 7519 apply. Possessing a key is only valuable if it is kept secret, so unintended parties must not learn private or symmetric key values. Applications using PoP should also use audience restriction: PoP lets a recipient reject messages from unauthorized senders, while audience restriction lets it reject messages meant for other recipients.

PoP via encrypted symmetric secrets is subject to replay attacks. This can be avoided with a signed nonce or challenge (a distinct one per interaction), or by deriving a sub-key from a shared secret specific to that PoP demonstration. A JWT still needs data origin authentication and integrity protection, and a symmetric key carried inside also needs confidentiality protection.

On privacy, a PoP key can act as a correlation handle if the same key is used with multiple parties. The RFC recommends different PoP keys for different parties.
sections.eli5: A secret only helps if it stays secret. Also, do not use the same secret handshake at every door, or the guards could compare notes and follow you around.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC registers the cnf claim (description "Confirmation", change controller IESG) in the IANA "JSON Web Token Claims" registry. It also creates a new "JWT Confirmation Methods" registry for members of the cnf object, and seeds it with jwk, jwe, kid and jku.

New values are registered on a Specification Required basis after a three-week review period, with Designated Experts. Because a goal is compact representations, names are RECOMMENDED not to exceed eight characters without a compelling reason.
sections.eli5: There is now an official list of the allowed ways to name the key, so new ideas can be added in an orderly way.
